chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ubayd Allah al-Dihqan, from Durust ibn Abi Mansur al-Wasiti, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said:

A man came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have taught this son of mine writing. In what trade should I entrust him?' He said: 'Entrust him to God, your father, and do not entrust him to five trades: do not entrust him to a seller of shrouds, a goldsmith, a butcher, a grocer, or a slave trader.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is the seller of shrouds?' He said: 'He is the one who sells shrouds and hopes for the death of my community, and the newborn from my community is more beloved to me than whatever the sun rises upon.' As for the goldsmith, he deals with the debt of my community. As for the butcher, he slaughters until mercy leaves his heart. As for the grocer, he hoards food for my community, and it is more beloved to God that the servant meets Him as a thief than that he meets Him having hoarded food for forty days. As for the slave trader, Gabriel came to me and said: 'O Muhammad, indeed the worst of your community are those who sell people.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: These two narrations are applicable to one who cannot ensure the trustworthiness and does not guard against defects in any of these trades. As for one who is careful, there is no harm upon him in any of them, although the best is the others.
ai.seo_question: What are the five trades a Muslim should avoid according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi contextualizes this narration by clarifying that the prohibition against these five trades—seller of shrouds, goldsmith, butcher, grocer, and slave trader—is primarily for those who cannot maintain spiritual vigilance, while those who preserve their piety are not strictly barred. The text highlights the ethical degradation inherent in these professions, such as the butcher's loss of mercy or the grocer's hoarding, linking them to broader themes of economic justice and character formation in Shia jurisprudence. This guidance underscores the importance of selecting livelihoods that nurture, rather than erode, one's moral and spiritual integrity.
